    Content from Shotgun metagenomics data to study the microbiome

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is the human gut microbiome and how can we study it with sequencing?
    • How does shotgun metagenomics differ from marker-gene (16S rRNA) sequencing?
    • What is the difference between taxonomic and functional profiling?
    • Which dataset will we use in this workshop, and how do we obtain it?

    Objectives

    • Understand the general concepts of the human gut microbiome
    • Distinguish shotgun metagenomics from marker-gene sequencing
    • Explain the difference between taxonomic and functional profiling
    • Map the main stages from FASTQ files to biological interpretation
    • Describe the workshop dataset and metadata
    • Download the workshop dataset and verify its integrity

    The human gut microbiome

    Shotgun metagenomics and marker-gene sequencing

    • Marker-gene sequencing amplifies and sequences one gene region (e.g. 16S rRNA, ITS).
    • Shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA in the sample.

    Taxonomic and functional profiling

    • Taxonomic profiling: which organisms are present and their abundance.
    • Functional profiling: which genes and metabolic pathways are present and their abundance.

    The workshop dataset

    5 simulated human gut metagenomes from Sun, Huang et al. (2021), with paired-end reads, ground-truth abundance tables and sample metadata. The true composition of each sample is known.

    First look at the reads

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    BASH 

    # number of reads in a file (lines / 4)
# PENDING TO WRITE CODE
    Key Points
    • Shotgun metagenomics sequences all DNA in a sample.
    • Taxonomic profiling describes which organisms are present; functional profiling describes their genes and pathways.
    • The workshop uses 5 simulated gut metagenomes with a known composition.

    Content from Reproducible workflows with Nextflow and nf-core

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Why is reproducibility a challenge in bioinformatics?
    • What are Nextflow and nf-core, and how do they help?
    • How do I connect to a Nectar instance and check that the software is available?
    • How do I prepare the input files needed by nf-core/taxprofiler and nf-core/funcprofiler?

    Objectives

    • Understand reproducibility in bioinformatics
    • Explain what Nextflow is and why it is useful
    • Navigate the nf-core website and find suitable pipelines
    • Connect to a Nectar instance
    • Load and check the software used in the workshop
    • Construct reproducible commands for both pipelines
    • Prepare and validate samplesheets and database sheets

    Reproducibility in bioinformatics

    Nextflow and nf-core

    • Nextflow: workflow manager.
    • nf-core: community-curated Nextflow pipelines.

    Pipelines are listed on the nf-core website. In this workshop we use:

    • nf-core/taxprofiler
    • nf-core/funcprofiler

    Connecting to Nectar

    BASH 

    ssh ubuntu@<IP_adress>
    Callout

    We already prepared the databases for this workshop. If you are following the workshop remotely, please download the databases for each chosen tool as well as modify the path accordingly.

    Loading the software

    Check that each tool is available:

    BASH 

    java -version
nextflow -version
apptainer --version
nf-core --version

    Preparing the samplesheet

    Both pipelines use the same samplesheet columns: sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta. Paths must be absolute.

    BASH 

    cd /mnt/data/taxprofiler

echo "sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta" > samplesheet.csv
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  echo "gut${i},run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample${i}_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample${i}_sub_R2.fastq.gz," >> samplesheet.csv
done
cat samplesheet.csv

    OUTPUT 

    sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta
gut1,run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample1_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample1_sub_R2.fastq.gz,
gut2,run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample2_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample2_sub_R2.fastq.gz,
gut3,run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample3_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample3_sub_R2.fastq.gz,
gut4,run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample4_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample4_sub_R2.fastq.gz,
gut5,run1,ILLUMINA,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample5_sub_R1.fastq.gz,/mnt/data/rawreads/Gut_sample5_sub_R2.fastq.gz,

    Check that every file listed exists:

    BASH 

    tail -n +2 samplesheet.csv | cut -d, -f4,5 | tr ',' '\n' | xargs ls -l

    Preparing the database sheets

    taxprofiler: databases_taxprofiler.csv

    Columns are tool,db_name,db_params,db_type,db_path.

    BASH 

    cat > databases_taxprofiler.csv << 'EOF'
tool,db_name,db_params,db_type,db_path
kraken2,k2_standard_08_GB_20260626,,short;long,/mnt/data/taxprofiler/databases/kraken2/k2_standard_08_GB_20260626
bracken,k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken,;-r 150,short,/mnt/data/taxprofiler/databases/kraken2/k2_standard_08_GB_20260626
motus,db_mOTU_v3.1.0,,short;long,/mnt/data/taxprofiler/databases/motus/db_mOTU
EOF

    funcprofiler: databases_funcprofiler.csv

    Columns are tool,db_name,db_entity,db_params,db_path. HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper need one row per database component.

    BASH 

    cat > databases_funcprofiler.csv << 'EOF'
tool,db_name,db_entity,db_params,db_path
diamond,gut_workshop_v1,,,/mnt/data/funcprofiler/databases/diamond
EOF

    Set the pipeline’s resource limits

    Nextflow does not know how many CPUs and how much memory your machine has. Therefore, a config file is needed to cap every task at what your machine actually has, so no step asks for more and fails. We will create a config file for Nectar. Again, if you are following this workshop remotely, modify the parameters in the following code that match with your machine.

    BASH 

    mkdir -p configs

CPUS=$(nproc) #number of CPUs
MEM=$(( $(free -g | awk '/^Mem:/{print $2}') - 2 )) #number of RAM minus 2 (always spare some for trivial tasks)

cat > configs/nectar.config <<EOF
workDir = '/mnt/data/taxprofiler/work'
process {
    resourceLimits = [ cpus: ${CPUS}, memory: '${MEM}.GB', time: '48.h' ]
}
executor {
    name   = 'local'
    cpus   = ${CPUS}
    memory = '${MEM}.GB'
}
EOF

    Reproducible launch commands

    Parameters go in a params.json file and the command in a launch script.

    BASH 

    cat > params_taxprofiler.json << EOF
{
  "input": "/mnt/data/taxprofiler/samplesheet.csv",
  "databases": "/mnt/data/taxprofiler/databases_taxprofiler.csv",
  "outdir": "/mnt/data/taxprofiler/results",
  "perform_shortread_qc": true,
  "save_analysis_ready_fastqs": true,
  "run_kraken2": true,
  "run_bracken": true,
  "run_metaphlan": false,
  "run_motus": true,
  "run_sylph": false,
  "run_profile_standardisation": true,
  "run_krona": true,
  "taxpasta_add_name": false,
  "taxpasta_add_rank": false,
  "taxpasta_add_lineage": false
}
EOF

    BASH 

    cat > nf_taxprofiler_launch.sh << 'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
nextflow run nf-core/taxprofiler \
  -r 2.0.1 \
  -profile docker \
  -c configs/nectar.config \
  -params-file params_taxprofiler.json \
  -resume
EOF
chmod +x nextflow_launch.sh

    Alternatively, the nf-core tools launcher writes a nf-params.json interactively:

    BASH 

    nf-core pipelines launch nf-core/taxprofiler -r <version>
    Key Points
    • Pin pipeline versions with -r.
    • Check software with nextflow -version and apptainer --version before launching.
    • Both pipelines need a samplesheet with absolute paths and a database sheet.
    • Keep parameters in params.json and the command in a launch script.

    Content from Taxonomic profiling with nf-core/taxprofiler

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I configure and run nf-core/taxprofiler?
    • How do sylph, mOTUs, Kraken2/Bracken and MetaPhlAn differ?
    • How do I interpret the pipeline outputs?
    • Which table do I need for downstream analysis in R?

    Objectives

    • Configure taxonomic profiling with nf-core/taxprofiler
    • Explain the roles of sylph, mOTUs, Kraken2/Bracken and MetaPhlAn
    • Interpret the MultiQC report, classification summaries and pipeline reports
    • Identify the standardised abundance table needed for downstream analysis

    The profilers

    • Kraken2 and Bracken
    • MetaPhlAn (we will not run this profiler during the workshop due, precomputed outputs will be provided)
    • mOTUs
    • sylph (we will not run this profiler during the workshop due, precomputed outputs will be provided)

    Running the pipeline

    BASH 

    cd /mnt/data/taxprofiler
./nextflow_launch.sh

    or directly:

    BASH 

    nextflow run nf-core/taxprofiler \
  -r 2.0.1 \
  -profile docker \
  --input samplesheet.csv \
  --databases databases_taxprofiler.csv \
  --outdir /mnt/data/taxprofiler/results \
  --perform_shortread_qc \
  --save_analysis_ready_fastqs \
  --run_kraken2 --run_bracken \
  --run_motus \
  --run_profile_standardisation \
  --run_krona \
  -resume

    Output overview

    BASH 

    ls /mnt/data/taxprofiler/results

    OUTPUT 

    analysis_ready_fastqs  bracken  fastp  kraken2  krona  motus
multiqc  pipeline_info

    MultiQC report

    multiqc/multiqc_report.html contains the read QC (fastp) and classification summaries. Copy it to your laptop to open it:

    BASH 

    # PENDING TO WRITE CODE

    Taxonomic classification summaries

    The pipeline writes one folder per profiler into results/:

    results/
├── kraken2
│   ├── k2_standard_08_GB_20260626
│   │   ├── Gut_sample1_Gut_sample1_run1_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626.kraken2.kraken2.report.txt
│   │   ├── ...                                   (one report per sample)
│   │   └── Gut_sample5_Gut_sample5_run1_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626.kraken2.kraken2.report.txt
│   ├── k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken
│   ├── kraken2_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken-bracken_combined_reports.txt
│   └── kraken2_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_combined_reports.txt
├── bracken
│   ├── bracken_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken_combined_reports.txt
│   └── k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken
│       ├── Gut_sample1_..._bracken.bracken.kraken2.report_bracken.txt
│       ├── Gut_sample1_..._bracken.bracken.tsv
│       └── ...                                   (two files per sample)
├── motus
│   ├── db_mOTU_v3.1.0
│   │   ├── Gut_sample1_Gut_sample1_run1_db_mOTU_v3.1.0.log
│   │   ├── Gut_sample1_Gut_sample1_run1_db_mOTU_v3.1.0.out
│   │   └── ...                                   (.log + .out per sample)
│   └── motus_db_mOTU_v3.1.0_combined_reports.txt
└── taxpasta
    ├── bracken_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken.tsv
    ├── kraken2_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626_bracken-bracken.tsv
    ├── kraken2_k2_standard_08_GB_20260626.tsv
    ├── metaphlan_mpa_vJun23_CHOCOPhlAnSGB_202403.tsv
    └── motus_db_mOTU_v3.1.0.tsv

    Standardised and merged tables (Taxpasta)

    Taxpasta converts the output of each profiler into one merged table per profiler and database, with taxa in rows and samples in columns. The tables are in taxpasta/.

    BASH 

    ls /mnt/data/taxprofilertaxprofiler/results/taxpasta/

    We import these tables into R in the episode Importing and exploring microbiome data with R.

    Pipeline execution and resource reports

    pipeline_info/ contains the execution report, timeline, trace and software versions.

    Key Points
    • nf-core/taxprofiler runs several profilers on the same pre-processed reads.
    • The Taxpasta tables are the input for the analysis in R.
    • pipeline_info/ records resource usage and software versions.

    Content from Functional profiling with nf-core/funcprofiler

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I configure and run nf-core/funcprofiler?
    • What do HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper measure?
    • What is the difference between gene-family abundance, pathway abundance and pathway coverage?

    Objectives

    • Configure functional profiling with nf-core/funcprofiler
    • Explain the roles of HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper
    • Distinguish gene-family abundance, pathway abundance and pathway coverage
    • Identify the standardised function tables needed for downstream analysis

    HUMAnN and eggNOG-mapper

    • HUMAnN
    • eggNOG-mapper

    Input: pre-processed reads

    nf-core/funcprofiler does not perform read QC or host removal. We use the reads saved by taxprofiler with --save_analysis_ready_fastqs. We work in the same folder as in the previous episodes, where the database sheets and the Nectar config file are:

    BASH 

    cd /mnt/data/taxprofiler
ls /mnt/data/taxprofiler/results/analysis_ready_fastqs/

    fastp names the cleaned reads <sample>_<run_accession>_1.fastp.fastq.gz and <sample>_<run_accession>_2.fastp.fastq.gz:

    BASH 

    READS=/mnt/data/taxprofiler/results/analysis_ready_fastqs
echo "sample,run_accession,instrument_platform,fastq_1,fastq_2,fasta" > samplesheet_func.csv
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  r1=$READS/gut${i}_run1_1.fastp.fastq.gz
  r2=$READS/gut${i}_run1_2.fastp.fastq.gz
  echo "gut${i},run1,ILLUMINA,${r1},${r2}," >> samplesheet_func.csv
done
cat samplesheet_func.csv

    Check that every file listed exists:

    BASH 

    tail -n +2 samplesheet_func.csv | cut -d, -f4,5 | tr ',' '\n' | xargs ls -l

    Running the pipeline

    During the workshop we run DIAMOND, the only database in databases_funcprofiler.csv. HUMAnN 4 and eggNOG-mapper need much larger databases and several hours, so their outputs have been precomputed for you.

    BASH 

    nextflow run nf-core/funcprofiler \
  -r 1.0.0 \
  -profile docker \
  -c configs/nectar.config \
  --input samplesheet_func.csv \
  --databases databases_funcprofiler.csv \
  --outdir /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results \
  --run_diamond \
  -resume

    Outputs

    BASH 

    ls /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results
ls /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results/diamond/gut_workshop_v1
ls /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results/humann4

    All outputs are in /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results/:

    • MultiQC report: multiqc/multiqc_report.html
    • DIAMOND alignments (run during the workshop): diamond/gut_workshop_v1/
    • HUMAnN 4 outputs (precomputed), one set of files per sample in humann4/:
      • Gene family abundance: <sample>_2_genefamilies.tsv.gz
      • Reaction abundance: <sample>_3_reactions.tsv.gz
      • Pathway abundance: <sample>_4_pathabundance.tsv.gz
      • Gene families regrouped to other functional categories: <sample>_regroup.tsv.gz
      • Species functional profiles: stratified rows (PATHWAY|g__Genus.s__species) in the HUMAnN tables
    • eggNOG-mapper annotations (precomputed): eggnogmapper/*.emapper.annotations
    • Execution and resource reports: pipeline_info/

    HUMAnN 4 does not write a separate pathway coverage table as HUMAnN 3 did.

    BASH 

    zcat /mnt/data/funcprofiler/results/humann4/Gut_sample1_4_pathabundance.tsv.gz | head -n 5

    The precomputed outputs use the sample names Gut_sample1 to Gut_sample5 instead of gut1 to gut5. A copy of the HUMAnN 4 outputs is also in /mnt/data/workshop_data/funcprofiler/humann4/, which is the folder we use in R.

    Key Points
    • nf-core/funcprofiler expects reads that have already been through QC.
    • HUMAnN reports gene families, pathway abundance and pathway coverage, overall and per species.

    Content from Importing and exploring microbiome data with R

    Last updated on 2026-11-03 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Which R data structures are used for microbiome data?
    • How do I import a taxonomic profile, a functional profile and sample metadata into R?
    • How do I aggregate, filter and transform microbiome data?

    Objectives

    • Identify the phyloseq and TreeSummarizedExperiment object types and explain their principal differences
    • Import a MetaPhlAn taxonomic profile, HUMAnN pathway abundances and the sample metadata
    • Build a TreeSummarizedExperiment object and explore its components
    • Aggregate taxa at a selected rank, filter low-prevalence features and calculate relative abundance
    • Visualise taxonomic composition, prevalence and the most abundant taxa and pathways

    In the previous episodes nf-core/taxprofiler and nf-core/funcprofiler produced several tables. Here we bring one taxonomic profile (MetaPhlAn) and one functional profile (HUMAnN pathway abundance) into R. We use them to build data objects that Bioconductor packages can work with, and to take a first look at the samples.

    Callout

    Where do we run R?

    We use the workshop RStudio Server, a separate Nectar instance from the one where we ran the pipelines. Copies of the pipeline outputs are already in /data/workshop_data/ on the RStudio Server, so we read them directly and do not need to copy anything.

    OUTPUT 

    /data/workshop_data
├── funcprofiler/humann4/        # HUMAnN 4 outputs, one set of files per sample
├── metadata/                    # samplesheets used to run the pipelines
└── taxprofiler/                 # Taxpasta tables and merged profiler reports

    Loading the libraries

    R 

    library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(SummarizedExperiment)
library(TreeSummarizedExperiment)
library(mia)
library(miaViz)

    Record the package versions. Function names in mia and miaViz have changed between releases, so this helps when you compare your code with other tutorials:

    R 

    packageVersion("mia")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '1.20.0'

    R 

    packageVersion("miaViz")

    OUTPUT 

    [1] '1.20.0'

    Then define where the data are:

    R 

    data_dir  <- "/data/workshop_data"
mpa_file  <- file.path(data_dir, "taxprofiler",
                       "metaphlan_mpa_vJun23_CHOCOPhlAnSGB_202403_combined_reports.txt")
meta_file <- file.path(data_dir, "metadata", "taxprofiler_samplesheet.csv")
humann_dir <- file.path(data_dir, "funcprofiler", "humann4")

# TRUE on the workshop RStudio Server, where all the input files are present.
# The lesson website is built without these files, so there the chunks that
# read the data are shown but not run.
has_data <- file.exists(mpa_file) &&
            file.exists(meta_file) &&
            length(list.files(humann_dir,
                              pattern = "_4_pathabundance\\.tsv\\.gz$")) > 0

    phyloseq and TreeSummarizedExperiment

    A microbiome dataset has three parts that must stay in sync: an abundance table (features × samples), information about the features (taxonomy, pathway names) and information about the samples (metadata). Two R object types keep these together:

    Component phyloseq TreeSummarizedExperiment (TSE)
    Abundance table otu_table() assay(), which can hold several (counts, relative abundance, …)
    Feature information tax_table() rowData()
    Sample information sample_data() colData()
    Phylogenetic tree phy_tree() rowTree()
    Other data types – altExp(), e.g. the same samples aggregated at another rank
    • phyloseq is the original microbiome package. Many older tutorials and packages use it.
    • TreeSummarizedExperiment builds on Bioconductor’s SummarizedExperiment, the same structure used for RNA-seq and other omics data. It can store several assays and alternative experiments in one object. The mia and miaViz packages and the Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis (OMA) book are built around it.

    We use TSE in this workshop. If you need phyloseq for another package, you can convert in both directions (this needs the phyloseq package installed):

    R 

    ps  <- convertToPhyloseq(tse)
tse <- convertFromPhyloseq(ps)

    Importing the taxonomic profile

    nf-core/taxprofiler ran four profilers. Here we use MetaPhlAn, because its merged report already contains the full lineage of each taxon (k__Bacteria|p__…|g__…|s__…). mia reads this format directly with importMetaPhlAn():

    R 

    tse <- importMetaPhlAn(mpa_file)
tse

    The object has one row per MetaPhlAn species-level genome bin (SGB, t__…) and one column per sample. importMetaPhlAn() also stored the profile aggregated at every taxonomic rank as alternative experiments (altExpNames).

    Tidying sample and taxon names

    The column names include the run and database names, and the samples are not in order. We keep only the sample ID and sort the samples:

    R 

    colnames(tse)
colnames(tse) <- sub("^(Gut_sample[0-9]+)_.*$", "\\1", colnames(tse))
tse <- tse[, sort(colnames(tse))]
colnames(tse)

    The taxon names have MetaPhlAn rank prefixes (g__, s__). We remove them so the plot labels are easier to read:

    R 

    for (r in taxonomyRanks(tse)) {
  rowData(tse)[[r]] <- sub("^[a-z]__", "", rowData(tse)[[r]])
}
rowData(tse)[1:3, c("phylum", "genus", "species")]

    Exploring the object

    Let’s look at the three main components:

    R 

    assayNames(tse)
assay(tse, "metaphlan")[1:5, ]
rowData(tse)[1:3, c("phylum", "genus", "species")]
taxonomyRanks(tse)

    MetaPhlAn reports relative abundance in percent, not read counts, so each sample sums to about 100:

    R 

    colSums(assay(tse, "metaphlan"))
    Callout

    What about sequencing depth?

    Because MetaPhlAn reports percentages, we cannot see how many reads each sample had. Use the fastp section of the taxprofiler MultiQC report for read numbers. Profilers that report read counts (Kraken2/Bracken, for example) are compared on Day 2.

    Adding the sample metadata

    We use the samplesheet given to the pipelines as sample metadata. We join it to the sample names of the TSE, so the order of the metadata always matches the order of the columns.

    Note the dplyr:: prefix. mia also has functions called left_join(), inner_join(), full_join() and right_join(). Because we loaded mia after dplyr, a plain left_join() would call the mia version, which fails on data frames.

    R 

    samplesheet <- read_csv(meta_file, show_col_types = FALSE)

col_df <- tibble(sample = colnames(tse)) |>
  dplyr::left_join(select(samplesheet, sample, run_accession, instrument_platform),
            by = "sample")

colData(tse) <- DataFrame(col_df, row.names = col_df$sample)
colData(tse)
    Callout

    Always check that the samples match

    If a sample name in the metadata is spelled differently from the one in the abundance table, left_join() silently fills that row with NA. Check this before continuing:

    R 

    stopifnot(!anyNA(colData(tse)$run_accession))

    Aggregating, filtering and transforming

    Three operations come before most microbiome analyses:

    1. Aggregate features at the taxonomic rank of interest. agglomerateByRank() sums the abundances of all rows that share the same genus (or phylum, …).
    2. Filter features that are rare across samples. subsetByPrevalent() keeps taxa that are above a detection threshold in more than a prevalence fraction of samples. Rare taxa add noise and many zeros to downstream statistics.
    3. Transform the abundances. transformAssay() adds a new assay next to the original, for example relative abundance (proportions between 0 and 1).

    R 

    tse_genus <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
dim(tse_genus)

    Keep genera with an abundance above 0.1 % in more than half of the samples (at least 3 of 5), then calculate relative abundance:

    R 

    tse_genus <- subsetByPrevalent(tse_genus,
                               assay.type = "metaphlan",
                               detection  = 0.1,
                               prevalence = 0.5)
tse_genus <- transformAssay(tse_genus,
                            assay.type = "metaphlan",
                            method     = "relabundance")
dim(tse_genus)
assayNames(tse_genus)
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: How strict is the filter?

    Starting again from agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus"), how many genera are kept if a genus must be above 0.1 % in all five samples? And in at least one sample?

    Hint: subsetByPrevalent() keeps features whose prevalence is strictly greater than prevalence. Look at the include.lowest argument in ?getPrevalence.

    R 

    tse_g <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
# All five samples
nrow(subsetByPrevalent(tse_g, assay.type = "metaphlan",
                       detection = 0.1, prevalence = 1,
                       include.lowest = TRUE))
# At least one sample
nrow(subsetByPrevalent(tse_g, assay.type = "metaphlan",
                       detection = 0.1, prevalence = 1/5,
                       include.lowest = TRUE))

    Without include.lowest = TRUE, prevalence = 1 returns no genera, because a prevalence can never be strictly greater than 100 %. The stricter the prevalence threshold, the fewer taxa remain. No single threshold is correct: it depends on the number of samples and on the question you are asking.

    Visualising composition

    Composition bar plot

    At phylum level a stacked bar plot gives an overview of each sample:

    R 

    tse_phylum <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "phylum")
tse_phylum <- transformAssay(tse_phylum, assay.type = "metaphlan",
                             method = "relabundance")
plotAbundance(tse_phylum, assay.type = "relabundance") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Relative abundance") +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(title = "Phylum"),
         colour = guide_legend(title = "Phylum")) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))

    Prevalence plot

    The prevalence plot shows how many genera remain at different detection thresholds (x axis) and prevalence thresholds (one line per prevalence, here 1 to 5 of the 5 samples). It helps when choosing a filter. The detection values are in percent, the units of the metaphlan assay:

    R 

    tse_g <- agglomerateByRank(tse, rank = "genus")
plotPrevalence(tse_g, assay.type = "metaphlan",
               detection = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10),
               prevalence = (1:5) / 5, include.lowest = TRUE) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Detection threshold (% abundance, log scale)", y = "Number of genera")

    Heatmap of the most abundant genera

    getTop() returns the names of the most abundant features. meltSE() turns the TSE into a long data frame that ggplot2 can use:

    R 

    top_genera <- getTop(tse_genus, top = 15, method = "mean",
                     assay.type = "relabundance")

meltSE(tse_genus[top_genera, ], assay.type = "relabundance") |>
  mutate(FeatureID = factor(FeatureID, levels = rev(top_genera))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = SampleID, y = FeatureID, fill = relabundance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Relative\nabundance") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "Genus") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

    Importing the functional profile

    HUMAnN writes one pathway abundance file per sample (*_4_pathabundance.tsv.gz). Each file has two columns: the pathway and its abundance. Some rows are special:

    • UNMAPPED: reads that did not map to any gene family.
    • UNINTEGRATED: gene families that could not be assigned to a pathway.
    • PATHWAY|g__Genus.s__species: stratified rows, which split the pathway’s abundance by contributing species.

    R 

    path_files <- list.files(humann_dir, pattern = "_4_pathabundance\\.tsv\\.gz$",
                         full.names = TRUE)
basename(path_files)
read_tsv(path_files[1], show_col_types = FALSE, n_max = 5)

    read_tsv() can read all files at once. The id argument records which file each row came from. We then keep only the community-level (unstratified) pathways and reshape the table to pathways × samples. Pathways missing from a sample get an abundance of 0:

    R 

    path_long <- read_tsv(path_files, id = "file", skip = 1,
                      col_names = c("pathway", "abundance"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(sample = sub("_4_pathabundance\\.tsv\\.gz$", "", basename(file))) |>
  filter(!grepl("|", pathway, fixed = TRUE),
         !pathway %in% c("UNMAPPED", "UNINTEGRATED"))

path_wide <- path_long |>
  select(pathway, sample, abundance) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sample, values_from = abundance, values_fill = 0)

path_mat <- as.matrix(path_wide[, -1])
rownames(path_mat) <- path_wide$pathway
path_mat <- path_mat[, colnames(tse)]   # same sample order as the taxonomic TSE
dim(path_mat)

    Now build a TSE directly with TreeSummarizedExperiment(), reusing the sample metadata of the taxonomic object. The HUMAnN abundances are not normalised, so we add relative abundance:

    R 

    tse_path <- TreeSummarizedExperiment(
  assays  = list(abundance = path_mat),
  colData = colData(tse)
)
tse_path <- transformAssay(tse_path, assay.type = "abundance",
                           method = "relabundance")
tse_path

    Heatmap of the most abundant pathways

    R 

    top_paths <- getTop(tse_path, top = 15, method = "mean",
                    assay.type = "relabundance")

meltSE(tse_path[top_paths, ], assay.type = "relabundance") |>
  mutate(FeatureID = factor(FeatureID, levels = rev(top_paths))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = SampleID, y = FeatureID, fill = relabundance)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Relative\nabundance") +
  labs(x = "Sample", y = "MetaCyc pathway") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Which pathways are most abundant?

    Which five pathways have the highest mean relative abundance? Are they the same in every sample?

    R 

    getTop(tse_path, top = 5, method = "mean", assay.type = "relabundance")

# Top pathway in each sample
apply(assay(tse_path, "relabundance"), 2, function(x) names(which.max(x)))

    The most abundant pathways are core housekeeping functions (peptidoglycan maturation, the pentose phosphate pathway, nucleotide biosynthesis and glycolysis), which many gut bacteria share. The same pathway is the most abundant in four of the five samples, although their taxonomic compositions differ a lot.

    Key Points
    • A TreeSummarizedExperiment keeps the abundance tables (assay), feature information (rowData) and sample information (colData) together. phyloseq objects can be converted to and from it.
    • importMetaPhlAn() reads a MetaPhlAn merged report, with the full taxonomy, into a TreeSummarizedExperiment.
    • HUMAnN pathway tables are read with readr, reshaped with tidyr and assembled with TreeSummarizedExperiment().
    • agglomerateByRank(), subsetByPrevalent() and transformAssay() aggregate, filter and transform the data.
    • Check that sample names match between abundance tables and metadata before any analysis.
